tier_reason: The README (README.org) shows the author's cargo bench output for scalar iterators versus faster's SIMD iterators; the benchmark code is public (benches/usage.rs, map_scalar and map_simd) and RUSTFLAGS target-cpu values are given, but the rustc nightly version is unstated and the host is named only as 'ivybridge' with no CPU model, so it falls short of A. First-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (author's 'extremely unscientific' cargo bench runs on an Ivy Bridge host): target-cpu=ivybridge (AVX): map_scalar 6,963 ns/iter vs map_simd 879 ns/iter (about 7.9x, derived from page data); reduce_scalar 6,905 vs reduce_simd 839 ns/iter (about 8.2x, derived from page data); target-cpu=x86-64 (SSE2): map 7,237 vs 1,879 ns/iter (about 3.9x, derived from page data); target-cpu=pentium (polyfills only): map 7,195 vs 6,271 ns/iter (about 1.15x, derived from page data). Some rows are slower with SIMD: zip_simd 1,128 vs zip_scalar 901 ns/iter on the AVX target; bench_determinant3_simd 593 vs 354 ns/iter and bench_nop_simd 69 vs 38 ns/iter on the pentium target.
corrections.workload: cargo bench over a 1024-element f32 array filled with -123.456 (benches/usage.rs). map_scalar computes 9*sqrt(ceil(recip(sqrt(sqrt(abs(v))))))-4-2 per element and collects into a Vec; map_simd computes 9*sqrt(ceil(rsqrt(sqrt(abs(v)))))-4-2 with faster's rsqrt, which on x86 is the approximate _mm256_rsqrt_ps/_mm_rsqrt_ps instruction, then scalar_collect. Built for ivybridge (AVX), x86-64 (SSE2) and pentium (polyfill only) targets on an Ivy Bridge host.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (Cargo.toml profile.release opt-level = 3) with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=ivybridge' / 'x86-64' / 'pentium'; requires a nightly rustc (src/lib.rs uses #![feature(stdsimd)] and #![feature(test)]), version not stated
corrections.caveats: The README calls its own benchmarks 'extremely unscientific'; single host named only as Ivy Bridge, rustc nightly version unstated. Unequal kernels: the SIMD map and reduce benchmarks call faster's rsqrt, which on x86 is the approximate _mm256_rsqrt_ps/_mm_rsqrt_ps (the trait documents significant error past 1e-3), while the scalar baseline does an exact sqrt().recip(), i.e. one extra sqrt and a division per element; the ceil() in the chain hides the approximation for the constant input -123.456, so results match, but part of the 7.9x comes from cheaper math rather than SIMD width alone. The input is a constant-filled 1024-element array. Some SIMD rows are slower than scalar (zip_simd on AVX, determinant3 and nop on the pentium polyfill target). The crate never built on stable Rust: it needs nightly with #![feature(stdsimd)] and packed_simd_2; the stdsimd feature gate was later removed from nightly, so it likely does not build on current toolchains (not built here). Last commit 2021-03-25; abandoned.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README exactly. Shortcomings to record: unequal kernels (approximate rsqrt intrinsic in the SIMD path versus exact sqrt plus reciprocal in the scalar baseline), self-described unscientific single-host runs without CPU model or rustc version, some SIMD rows slower than scalar, nightly-only crate on the removed stdsimd feature and packed_simd_2, abandoned since 2021. Metadata checked: MPL-2.0, 1.6k stars, not archived, last commit 2021-03-25.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: the README's AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl section names the CPU (Graviton4) and compiler (GCC 12), the flags are in the public CMakeLists.txt (Release, effective -O2, plus -march=native -fopenmp for GCC), and the benchmark code is public (reduce_bench.cpp registering unrolled_gt, stl_accumulate_gt, neon and sve kernels from reduce_cpu.hpp; Google Benchmark, MinTime 10 s, real time, result error checked against n*1.0). Same basis as the wave 11 intel/parallelstl entry, which was verified A on this README's Graviton4 table.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single thread versus serial std::accumulate (libstdc++, GCC 12), 1 GB array of 1.0f, README tables. AWS Graviton4 c8g.metal-24xl: unrolled/f64 14.7387 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f64 5.58465 GB/s (about 2.6x, derived from page data, both exact); unrolled/f32 28.2311 GB/s, neon/f32 22.2544 GB/s and sve/f32 21.4542 GB/s vs std::accumulate/f32 5.58767 GB/s (about 5.1x, 4.0x and 3.8x, derived from page data). AWS Zen4 m7a.metal-48xl: unrolled<f64> 34.0189 GB/s and avx2<f64> 19.3258 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f64> 4.88389 GB/s (about 7.0x and 4.0x, derived from page data, exact); unrolled<f32> 35.1514, avx2<f32> 33.3195 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.8351 GB/s vs std::accumulate<f32> 4.88655 GB/s (about 7.2x, 6.8x and 5.5x, derived from page data); avx2<f32kahan> 9.73619 GB/s, exact, about 2.0x std::accumulate (derived from page data). Nvidia DGX-H100 host: avx2<f32> 9.69112 vs std::accumulate<f32> 5.5322 GB/s (about 1.75x, derived from page data). Multithreaded std::reduce<par> (368.528 GB/s on Zen4, 550.384 GB/s on Graviton4) is libstdc++'s own parallel algorithm on oneTBB, not this repository's code.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 12 (NVCC 12.1 for the CUDA rows); CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release and appends -O2 to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE (effective -O2) and sets -march=native -fopenmp for GCC; the Apple M2 Pro table names no compiler
corrections.hardware: AWS Graviton4 (c8g.metal-24xl, 96 cores), AWS m7a.metal-48xl (AMD Zen4, 192 threads at 3701.95 MHz; CPU model string not printed), Nvidia DGX-H100 node (160 threads at 2100 MHz; CPU model not named), Apple M2 Pro
corrections.workload: Summing a 1 GB array (268,435,456 floats, all set to 1.0f by std::fill_n) with serial std::accumulate, an 8-accumulator unrolled loop, hand-written SSE/AVX2/AVX-512, NEON and SVE kernels, OpenMP, fork_union, Taskflow, std::reduce with execution policies, Thrust, CUB and CUDA kernels, reported in bytes/s with an error% column against the exact sum n.
corrections.caveats: This is an educational benchmark collection, not a reusable library, and it has no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404, no licence in the GitHub sidebar or Cargo.toml), so it is reference only. The baseline is std::accumulate, whose required left-to-right fold is latency-bound on the float add chain at -O2 without -ffast-math; most of the gain comes from reassociation with multiple accumulators, and no single-threaded std::reduce (or unseq) row is measured, which is the standard library's own reassociating alternative. Hand-written intrinsics do not beat the plain unrolled C++ loop in most tables: on Zen4 avx2<f32> 33.32, avx2<f64> 19.33 and avx512<f32interleaving> 26.84 GB/s are all below unrolled<f32> 35.15 / unrolled<f64> 34.02 GB/s, and on Graviton4 neon/f32 22.25 and sve/f32 21.45 GB/s are below unrolled/f32 28.23 GB/s, contradicting the README's statement that hand-written AVX2 beats auto-vectorization (it holds only on the DGX-H100 host). All f32 rows give wrong sums because the input is 2^28 ones and each f32 accumulator saturates at 2^24 (std::accumulate<f32> 93.75% error, unrolled<f32> 50%, neon/sve 75%); only f64 and Kahan rows are exact, and avx2<f32kahan> is about 2x std::accumulate on Zen4. The DGX-H100 table's std::reduce<par, f64> and <par_unseq, f64> rows report 100% error. The Zen4 and DGX tables use older row labels and predate the 2025 code. Single hand-pasted runs with no variance. The README's own conclusion is that multithreaded std::reduce is the CPU winner.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README; ratios corrected to be marked derived and extended with the exact f64 rows and the Graviton4 table, and the multithreaded std::reduce figure is attributed to libstdc++ rather than this repo. Shortcomings to record: no license (reference only), educational benchmark repo rather than a library, latency-bound std::accumulate baseline with no std::reduce single-thread row, hand-written SIMD kernels slower than the plain unrolled loop on Zen4 and Graviton4, all f32 rows wrong by 50-94% (only f64/Kahan exact), single runs. Overlap: the same README is the evidence behind the wave 11 intel/parallelstl entry (std::reduce<par>) and contains fork_union rows (wave 11 ashvardanian/fork_union); this record is distinct (its own kernels), not a duplicate. Metadata checked: 119 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-07-22 (stale).
